title: Subjunctive: opinion, doubt and purpose
objectives: I can express necessity, probability and judgment with impersonal expressions such as é importante que and é pena que.
I can contrast doubt and certainty: duvido que and não acho que with the subjunctive, acho que and tenho certeza de que with the indicative, and explain why the mood changes.
I can use para que, caso, embora, a menos que, sem que, contanto que and antes que with the subjunctive.
I can give advice and recommendations with recomendar que, sugerir que and aconselhar.
I can explain why the new words carry the accents they do, and why c, g and ç change spelling in subjunctive forms.

vocabulary.note: Ends in ão, a nasal diphthong (the tilde marks nasality, not stress). The ending ão predicts stress on the last syllable, o-pi-ni-ÃO, so no accent is written.

example.target: Na minha opinião, o filme é ótimo.
example.source: In my opinion, the movie is great.

vocabulary.note: The ending r predicts stress on the last syllable, du-vi-DAR, so no accent. The related noun is written dúvida, DÚ-vi-da, with an accent because its stress is on the third to last syllable. The verb already means that the speaker does not commit to the clause, so it takes the subjunctive without any negation.

example.target: Duvido que ele chegue a tempo.
example.source: I doubt he will arrive on time.
example.source_literal: I-doubt that he arrive at time.

vocabulary.note: The c before e is [s], and a z between vowels is [z]: cer-TE-za. Ter certeza de que is followed by the indicative, because the speaker commits to the clause. In speech people often drop de: Tenho certeza que ela vem.

example.target: Tenho certeza de que ela vai gostar.
example.source: I'm sure she will like it.
example.source_literal: I-have certainty of that she is-going to-like.

vocabulary.note: The c before r is hard, [k], because c is soft only before e or i. It is the loosest of the commitment verbs: a speaker who hedges may use the subjunctive even in the affirmative.

example.target: Acredito que o preço vai cair.
example.source: I believe the price will fall.

vocabulary.note: The ch is one sound, [ʃ], like English sh. Achar literally means to find (achei a chave, I found the key). As a verb of opinion, acho que is I find that, that is, it seems to me. Acho que takes the indicative; não acho que takes the subjunctive.

example.target: Acho que você tem razão.
example.source: I think you are right.

vocabulary.note: Portuguese has no empty subject word like English it: the verb é stands alone. The im before p is a nasal vowel (the m is the spelling used before p and b), and the final te is said [tʃi]. Followed by the subjunctive because the speaker evaluates the clause.

example.target: É importante que você leia o contrato.
example.source: It is important that you read the contract.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable, ne-ces-SÁ-ri-o, because the ending io counts as two syllables. No ending predicts that stress, so the acute accent is always written. The ss is [s].

example.target: É necessário que todos cheguem no horário.
example.source: It is necessary that everyone arrive on time.
example.source_literal: Is necessary that all arrive in-the schedule.

vocabulary.note: The ending l predicts stress on the last syllable, but the word is said pos-SÍ-vel, one syllable earlier, so the í is written. The ss is [s] and the final l is said [w].

example.target: É possível que eles saiam cedo.
example.source: It's possible that they will leave early.

vocabulary.note: Same pattern as possível: pro-VÁ-vel is stressed one syllable before the last, so the á is written; it is an open a, as in father. Likelihood is a degree below fact, so it takes the subjunctive.

example.target: É provável que chova à tarde.
example.source: It is likely to rain in the afternoon.
example.source_literal: Is probable that it-rain to-the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Pena is a noun meaning pity or sorrow; the same word also means feather and penalty. The speaker already knows the fact and is reacting to it, which is why the subjunctive follows.

example.target: É pena que você não possa vir.
example.source: It's a pity you can't come.
example.source_literal: Is pity that you not can come.

vocabulary.note: Melhor is the comparative of bom (good). The ending r predicts stress on the last syllable, me-LHOR, and the lh is one sound, [ʎ], like the lli of million. A soft way to give advice.

example.target: É melhor que a gente saia cedo.
example.source: It is better that we leave early.
example.source_literal: Is better that the-people leave early.

vocabulary.note: The c before o is hard, [k]. The em is a nasal vowel, and the ending r puts the stress on the last syllable: re-co-men-DAR.

example.target: Recomendo que você visite o museu.
example.source: I recommend that you visit the museum.

vocabulary.note: The g before e or i is soft, [ʒ]. In the eu form the stem vowel e becomes i: sugiro. The subjunctive copies the eu form, so it is sugira, sugiramos; the forms sugere and sugerimos keep the e.

example.target: Sugiro que a gente marque outro dia.
example.source: I suggest that we pick another day.
example.source_literal: I-suggest that the-people mark another day.

vocabulary.note: Built on the noun conselho. The lh is one sound, [ʎ], and the on is nasal. Also used with an object and a: Aconselho você a esperar.

example.target: Aconselho você a esperar mais um pouco.
example.source: I advise you to wait a little longer.
example.source_literal: I-advise you to wait more a little.

vocabulary.note: Countable, unlike English advice: um conselho, dois conselhos. The s after the nasal on is [s], not [z], because it does not stand between two vowel sounds: con-SE-lho. The lh is one sound, [ʎ].

example.target: Posso te dar um conselho?
example.source: Can I give you some advice?

vocabulary.note: The prefix des- reverses a word: igualdade is equality. In gual the u is pronounced ([gw]), because gu is silent only before e or i. The syllable-final l is said [w], and the final de is [dʒi]: de-si-gual-DA-de.

example.target: A desigualdade é um grande desafio no Brasil.
example.source: Inequality is a major challenge in Brazil.

vocabulary.note: Des- plus emprego (job). The s between vowels is [z], and the em before p is nasal: de-zem-PRE-go.

example.target: O desemprego afeta muitas famílias.
example.source: Unemployment affects many families.

vocabulary.note: Covers both safety and security. The g before u is hard, and this u is pronounced as a vowel, se-gu-RAN-ça. The ç is [s] before a, and the an is nasal.

example.target: A segurança nas ruas preocupa os moradores.
example.source: Safety on the streets worries the residents.

vocabulary.note: Always takes the subjunctive. The em before b is nasal: em-BO-ra. As an adverb it means away (ir embora, to leave), and historically it comes from em boa hora, in a good hour.

example.target: Embora seja caro, o curso vale a pena.
example.source: Although it is expensive, the course is worth it.
example.source_literal: Although be expensive, the course is-worth the pain.

vocabulary.note: The u of qu is silent. Que is [ke] when stressed, but as a small unstressed word, as here, it is usually said [ki]. In speech para becomes pra.

example.target: Trabalho muito para que meus filhos estudem.
example.source: I work hard so that my children can study.
example.source_literal: I-work much for that my children study.

vocabulary.note: The s between vowels is [z]: CA-zo. Introduces a possibility and always takes the subjunctive. The same word is the noun caso, case. Common in customer service and signs.

example.target: Caso chova, o show será no teatro.
example.source: In case it rains, the show will be in the theater.
example.source_literal: Case it-rain, the show will-be in-the theater.

vocabulary.note: Menos (less) is said [ˈmenus]: the final o is weak. The clause names the only exception to the main clause.

example.target: Vamos sair às oito, a menos que você prefira mais cedo.
example.source: We'll leave at eight, unless you prefer earlier.
example.source_literal: We-go leave at-the eight, at less that you prefer more early.

vocabulary.note: The em in sem is a nasal vowel with a glide, [sẽj̃]. Used when the two clauses have different subjects; with the same subject use sem plus an infinitive (saí sem comer).

example.target: Não faço nada sem que você saiba.
example.source: I don't do anything without you knowing.
example.source_literal: Not I-do nothing without that you know.

vocabulary.note: Built from com plus tanto. The on and an are nasal, because each n ends a syllable: con-TAN-to.

example.target: Eu empresto o carro, contanto que você devolva hoje.
example.source: I'll lend you the car, provided you return it today.
example.source_literal: I lend the car, with-so-much that you return today.

vocabulary.note: The an is nasal, and the t before the weak e of the ending es is said [tʃ], like the ch of cheese: [ˈɐ̃tʃis]. With the same subject use antes de plus an infinitive.

example.target: Vamos embora antes que o tempo piore.
example.source: Let's leave before the weather gets worse.
example.source_literal: We-go away before that the weather worsen.

vocabulary.note: The ç is [s] before ã, and the ão is a nasal diphthong. The ending predicts stress on the last syllable, con-di-ÇÃO, so no accent is needed. The d before i is said [dʒ], like the j of jeans.

example.target: A condição é que você chegue cedo.
example.source: The condition is that you arrive early.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in this unit's words
grammar.explanation:
Spelling is a code for sound, and the accent marks are part of that code, as the lessons on sounds and on stress showed. Three facts from those lessons are all you need here. Every word has one stressed syllable, the one said louder and longer. The ending of a word predicts which syllable that is: words ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words ending in l, r, z, i or u (with or without a final s), or a nasal ã or ão, are stressed on the last. A written accent appears when a word breaks the prediction of its ending, and it sits on the stressed vowel. The acute accent (´) on a, e or o shows an open vowel, the circumflex (^) shows a closed one, and on i and u the acute only marks stress. The procedure for any word is: divide it into syllables, find the stress by ear, read the default from the ending, compare.

The first group here is words that end in l but are stressed one syllable earlier: possível, provável, flexível, difícil. The ending l predicts the last syllable, pos-si-VEL. But the words are said pos-SÍ-vel, pro-VÁ-vel, di-FÍ-cil, with the stress one syllable earlier than the ending predicts, so the accent marks the exception. An English speaker is tempted to stress the last syllable, and the accent is exactly the mark that says not to.

The second group is words stressed on the third to last syllable, called proparoxytones. No ending predicts that stress, so these words always carry an accent: ótimo, sábado, público, últimos, dúvidas, óbvio, trânsito, médico, ônibus. Ônibus ends in us, which would predict the last syllable, but it is said Ô-ni-bus. The mark follows the vowel quality: ó and á are open, and ú only marks stress. Trânsito has a circumflex because â is a closed a before an n or m, as in câmera and lâmpada. Words ending in a glide plus a vowel belong here too: in necessário, voluntário, horário and escritório the ending io counts as two syllables, so ne-ces-SÁ-ri-o is stressed on the third to last syllable, exactly like história and família in the earlier lesson.

A third group is accents written for other reasons. Ninguém is said nin-GUÉM: the ending em predicts the second to last syllable, so stress on the last needs an accent, as in também. Já, é and vá are stressed one-syllable words ending in a or e, which take an accent; the one on é also separates the verb is from the unstressed word e, and. Saúde and açaí keep the accent on ú and í because the accent shows a hiatus, a stressed vowel that is alone in its syllable (sa-Ú-de, a-ça-Í). The words opinião, condição, previsão and manhã need no accent: the ending ã or ão predicts the last syllable, and the tilde shows nasality, not stress.

Finally, the grave accent in à and in vamos à praia or à tarde is not a stress mark. It writes the merger of the preposition a (to, at) with the article a (the): a + a = à, and a + as = às in às oito horas (at eight o'clock), and a + os = aos in aos sábados, as the lesson on accents explained.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: nasal vowels, lh, gu, ç and other letters in the new words
grammar.explanation:
The same principle governs every letter: a letter, or a pair of letters, stands for a small set of sounds, and something you can see decides which one. The next letter, the position in the word, or a mark settles it. This note applies the rules from the lesson on sounds to the words of this unit.

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by m or n that ends its syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not said as a consonant: im-por-TAN-te, con-SE-lho, em-PRE-go, con-TAN-to, an-tes, em-BO-ra. The spelling rule is that m is written before p and b, and n elsewhere. The tilde does the same job in ã and ão: opinião, condição, previsão, manhã. The final em of sem and ninguém is nasal with a small glide, [sẽj̃].

The letters c and g. The next letter decides: before e or i they are soft (c is [s], g is [ʒ], the sound of s in measure), and before a, o, u or a consonant they are hard. So certeza and ciclovia have [s], while recomendar, acreditar and segurança have [k] and [g]. The cedilla ç gives [s] before a, o, u: segurança, condição. To get a hard g before e or i, Portuguese writes gu and the u is normally silent: ninguém, aluguel (a few words such as aguentar and linguiça pronounce it). Before a, o or a consonant the u is a real vowel: in desigualdade it is said [gw], and in segurança the u is a vowel of its own.

The pairs lh, nh and ch are one sound each, never a letter followed by h: conselho and melhor have [ʎ], like the lli of million; venha and manhã have [ɲ], like the ny of canyon; achar, chova and chateado have [ʃ], like English sh. A single s between vowels is [z] (caso, desemprego, previsão, pousada), while ss is [s] (possível, necessário). At the start of a word, ex before a vowel is usually said with x = [z] (exato), and ex before a consonant with x = [s] (experimente). The h is never pronounced (honesto).

Finally, two position rules of Brazilian speech. In most of Brazil, a t or d before an i, including the weak e that is said [i], becomes [tʃ] or [dʒ]: antes, condição, verdade, desigualdade. And an l that closes a syllable is said [w]: desigualdade, aluguel, possível. The unstressed final vowels are weak: caso is [ˈkazu] and menos is [ˈmenus].

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why subjunctive forms change their consonant
grammar.explanation:
The present subjunctive is built from the eu form of the present: drop the final -o and add the opposite vowel, -e for -ar verbs and -a for -er and -ir verbs. Swapping that last vowel changes the letter that follows the end of the stem (the part of the verb that stays the same), and in Portuguese the letter after c or g decides how it sounds. The spelling therefore has to adjust so that the stem keeps its sound in every form. English does the same thing when picnic becomes picnicking, with a k added so that the c stays [k].

In -ar verbs the ending is -e, which is a soft-making vowel. A stem ending in a hard c or g would turn soft, so the spelling adds a u: c becomes qu and g becomes gu. Ficar gives fico but fique, and chegar gives chego but chegue, pagar gives pague, marcar gives marque. A stem ending in ç cannot keep it before e, because ç is written only before a, o and u, so it becomes c: começo but comece.

In -er and -ir verbs the ending is -a, which is a hard-making vowel, so a hard c or g needs no help and ç stays: faço gives faça, conheço gives conheça, ofereço gives ofereça. The reverse problem appears for verbs whose infinitive has a soft g, like dirigir and exigir. Their eu form is already written with j, dirijo and exijo, because go would be hard, and the subjunctive copies it: dirija, exija.

Since the subjunctive copies the eu form, every stem change in the eu form appears in all persons of the subjunctive. Sugerir has the vowel change e to i in the eu form, sugiro, so the subjunctive is sugira, sugiramos, sugiram. The same holds for leio and leia, vejo and veja, tenho and tenha, venho and venha. Verbs whose subjunctive does not come from the eu form are learned one by one: saiba, seja, esteja, vá. The j of seja and esteja is used because g before a would be hard, and j is always [ʒ]. The accent on vá follows the rule for stressed one-syllable words ending in a.

grammar.title: Impersonal expressions of judgment and necessity
grammar.explanation:
Start with the structure. A clause is a group of words built around one verb. Many sentences join two clauses with que (that): a main clause, which could stand alone, and a subordinate clause, which depends on it. In É importante que você leia o contrato, the main clause is É importante (it is important) and the subordinate clause is que você leia o contrato (that you read the contract). This note is about main clauses of the form é plus an adjective or noun. They are called impersonal because no particular person is the subject. English fills the empty subject position with the dummy word it; Portuguese has no such word, and the verb é stands alone.

The principle is that the mood of the subordinate clause records what the speaker is doing with it. The previous unit introduced the subjunctive as the mood used when the speaker does not simply pass information along. Here, the speaker is evaluating, requiring, or weighing a possibility. The indicative is the mood of reporting what the speaker treats as established. So the test is never whether the clause is true, but what the speaker is doing with it. In É pena que você não possa vir, both people know you cannot come; the sentence exists to express regret, so the subjunctive is used. In É verdade que ele mora em Recife, the sentence exists to confirm a fact, so the indicative is used.

Expressions of judgment, necessity and probability take the subjunctive: é importante, é necessário, é preciso, é bom, é melhor, é possível, é provável, é pena, é natural. Even é provável, which sounds close to certain, is a likelihood and therefore a degree below fact. Expressions that state or confirm a fact take the indicative: é verdade, é claro, é certo, é evidente, é óbvio, é fato. Negation removes the confirmation, so Não é verdade que ele more aqui, which denies, takes the subjunctive. The present subjunctive refers to the present or the future: É importante que você leia hoje and É importante que você leia amanhã.

The que clause is needed only to name who does the action. For a general statement, use the infinitive with no que: É importante estudar. When a person is named, add que and the subjunctive: É importante que você estude. English makes a similar choice with it is important to study versus it is important that you study. In everyday speech Brazilians also say Tem que chegar cedo (literally, has that arrive early), using an impersonal tem que. Pena is a noun, so É uma pena que... is also common.

grammar.title: Doubt versus certainty; negative and questioned opinion
grammar.explanation:
The principle is that a verb of thinking, believing or doubting reports how committed the speaker is to the que clause. Full commitment (I think, I believe, I am sure) treats the clause as information and takes the indicative. No commitment (I doubt, I don't think, I'm not sure) does not put the clause forward as true, so it takes the subjunctive. The mood works like a switch, set by the main verb and by negation, and the positions are the same as in the previous note: indicative when you assert, subjunctive when you do not.

English hides this switch, because it uses the same verb form in both cases: I think he is right, I don't think he is right. Portuguese shows the difference: Acho que ele tem razão, Não acho que ele tenha razão. It helps to know that achar literally means to find (as in finding a wallet), so acho que is I find that. The verb of commitment is a judgment, and negating the judgment is what flips the mood.

Verbs of commitment take the indicative: achar, acreditar, pensar, saber, ver, perceber, ter certeza de que, parece que. Expressions of non-commitment take the subjunctive: duvidar que, negar que, não achar que, não acreditar que, não ter certeza de que, não parecer que. Duvidar needs no negation, because its own meaning already withholds commitment. Where the negation sits matters: Acho que ele não vem (I think he isn't coming) stays indicative, because the negation is inside the que clause and the speaker still commits to something, while Não acho que ele venha negates the thinking verb itself.

There are degrees. Acreditar is the loosest of the commitment verbs, and a speaker who hedges may use the subjunctive even without a negation: Acredito que seja verdade. In a question, Você acha que ela vem? is neutral, asks for the other person's opinion and takes the indicative, which is by far the most common form. A question that signals disbelief can take the subjunctive: Você acredita que isso seja possível? In casual speech the indicative sometimes appears after não acho que, but careful writing uses the subjunctive. Note that se (whether) introduces an indirect question, which is a question reported inside a longer sentence instead of asked directly, and it takes the indicative: Não sei se ela vem (I don't know whether she is coming).

grammar.title: Conjunctions that require the subjunctive
grammar.explanation:
A conjunction is a word or short phrase that joins two clauses and names the relationship between them: purpose, condition, time, concession. Read word by word, most of these are a preposition or adverb plus que: para que (for that), sem que (without that), antes que (before that), a menos que (at less that), contanto que (with so much that). Caso and embora stand alone. Seeing the parts shows que doing the job it does everywhere, linking a clause.

What they share explains the mood. The clause they introduce is not reported as a fact that has happened: it is a purpose that may not be reached (para que), an event the speaker declares absent (sem que), something still ahead of the main event (antes que), an exception (a menos que), a condition (contanto que, caso). Because the event is unrealized, hypothetical or denied, the subjunctive is used. You can predict the mood from the meaning and learn the group as one family. English does the same job with ordinary verbs, so the difference is new to you: so that everyone understands uses a plain present verb, where Portuguese uses the subjunctive.

Embora is the case that teaches. A concession is a clause that admits a fact which seems to work against the main clause, as although does in English. After although the clause often states something true: the course is expensive, and the speaker knows it. But the clause presents the fact as background that the speaker admits and does not rely on; the point of the sentence is the main clause. Compare mas (but), which joins two assertions and takes the indicative: O curso é caro, mas vale a pena.

When the subject of both clauses is the same person, Portuguese prefers a preposition with the infinitive: Estudo para passar, Saí sem comer, Saí antes de comer. The conjunction with que is needed when the subjects differ or the clause names its own subject: Estudo para que você passe, Vamos sair antes que anoiteça. A menos que, contanto que, caso and embora have no infinitive partner and always take the subjunctive. In speech para becomes pra. Caso is common in service language: Caso tenha dúvidas, entre em contato. Both caso and se express conditions; se takes a different verb form, taught in a later unit.

grammar.title: Advice, recommendations and feelings about another person's action
grammar.explanation:
The principle is that verbs of influence express a wish about another person's action. When you recommend, suggest, advise, ask, demand, allow or forbid, the action you have in mind has not happened and might never happen; it exists only as your wish. That is the same not-yet-real logic as before, so the subjunctive follows. These verbs need two different people: the one who influences, who is the subject of the main verb, and the one influenced, who is the subject of the que clause. Sugiro que você descanse (I suggest that you rest).

There are three patterns. First, que plus the subjunctive: Recomendo que você visite o museu. Second, a person plus an infinitive, which is often more natural in speech: Aconselho você a esperar (I advise you to wait), Pedi pra ele esperar, Meu chefe me permite sair cedo. Third, the infinitive alone when there is no second person, or for a general recommendation: Recomendo visitar o museu. The choice between the first two is one of register, and both are correct.

Direct commands sound harsh between people who do not know each other well, so Brazilians soften advice. One way is the impersonal judgments from the first note: É melhor que você descanse, É bom que você durma cedo. Another is the suggestion Que tal descansar um pouco? (literally, what such to rest a little?), which takes a noun or an infinitive. A third is a negative question: Por que você não tenta de novo? (literally, for what you not try of new?). The subjunctive itself is a softener, because it frames the advice as a possibility rather than an order.

The same logic covers feelings and hopes about what another person does or will do. The feeling is a reaction to something the speaker does not simply report, so the subjunctive follows: Tenho medo que ele fique chateado (I have fear that he stays annoyed), Espero que você goste (I hope that you like it), Fico feliz que você possa vir. In Tenho medo que, writing de que is more formal; speech usually drops de.

In English, advice is uncountable: you cannot say an advice. Portuguese conselho is countable: um conselho, dois conselhos, dar um conselho (literally, to give a counsel).

culture.title: Giving opinions politely in Brazil
culture.text:
Brazilians love to discuss football, politics and daily life, and a lively exchange of opinions is a normal part of a meal or a bus ride. Yet directness is softened with phrases built on the subjunctive. Pode ser que você tenha razão (literally, can be that you have reason, meaning you may be right) always introduces a possibility and takes the subjunctive, because the speaker leaves the question open instead of asserting anything. Other softeners are Não sei se concordo (I'm not sure I agree; se means whether, so there is no mood switch) and Respeito sua opinião, mas...

When giving advice, people avoid orders and prefer suggestions: Sugiro que, Que tal, Por que você não...? A direct Você tem que... (literally, you have that...) can sound bossy among people who do not know each other well. The subjunctive helps here too, because it frames advice as a hope rather than a command. Among friends, strong opinions are expressed with teasing and humor, and disagreement is not usually taken personally.

Social issues such as desigualdade, violência, educação and saúde pública are regular topics in the news and in conversation. People often use the expression jeitinho brasileiro, literally the Brazilian little way, from jeito (a way or knack) with the diminutive ending -inho, to describe informal, flexible solutions to problems, and opinions about it range from admiration to criticism. In formal writing and customer service, caso is common: Caso tenha dúvidas, entre em contato (literally, case you have doubts, enter in contact).

exercises.audio_target: Trabalho para que meus filhos estudem.
choices: I work so that my children can study.
I work although my children study.
I work without my children studying.

exercises.prompt_source: I will go unless it rains.
answers: Eu vou, a menos que chova.
Eu vou a menos que chova.

exercises.audio_target: Embora seja difícil, vale a pena.
exercises.hint_source: Although it's hard, it's worth it.
